Skill Demand and Supply in Poland 2025

Insights from Online Job Postings and Trainings

Published

May 28, 2026

Executive Summary

Executive Summary

This report provides an evidence-based assessment of skill demand and training supply in Poland in 2025, combining large-scale online job-posting data from Pracuj.pl with training-service data from Baza Usług Rozwojowych (BUR). The analysis treats online vacancies as a timely proxy for employer demand and BUR listings as a proxy for the publicly visible, subsidised training supply. Both sources are transformed into comparable skill measures using NLP methods and mapped mainly to the ESCO taxonomy, with Lightcast used to capture more granular AI-related skill signals. The focus is compositional: the report compares the distribution of skills demanded by employers with the distribution of skills supplied through training, rather than attempting to compare the absolute number of vacancies with the number of training participants.

The main finding is that Poland’s training supply only partially matches the structure of employer demand. Employer demand is concentrated in management, communication, collaboration, digital, ICT, and business-administration skills. BUR training provision, by contrast, is relatively more concentrated in assisting and caring, machinery-related, services, health, and welfare skills. The resulting mismatch is moderate at the broad ESCO pillar level and more substantial at the more granular sub-group level, suggesting that the policy challenge is not only to expand training provision but to reallocate part of the training portfolio toward the skills most demanded in market-based hiring.

Digital and AI skills emerge as central areas of demand. Among classified digital skill mentions, advanced digital skills account for the largest share, followed by basic and intermediate skills. This suggests that digitalisation in Poland is not limited to basic ICT adoption; many employers are already seeking higher-order digital capabilities. AI-related demand remains small in total job postings under a conservative matching approach, but it is concentrated in knowledge-intensive services, especially professional, scientific, technical, telecommunications, IT, and information services. This pattern points to an early-stage but strategically important AI labour market, where demand is still narrow but likely to be important for productivity growth and competitiveness.

Green skills are present but still moderate in scale. Regional green-skill demand varies within a relatively narrow range, while sectoral intensity is highest in utilities, energy, agriculture, and public administration. In absolute terms, however, green demand is largest in large-employment sectors such as trade, professional services, and manufacturing. This distinction is important for policy: sector-specific green transition strategies should target high-intensity sectors, but large-scale upskilling efforts should also account for sectors where green skills are less concentrated but affect many workers.

The report also highlights the importance of migration and care-related labour needs. Postings explicitly tagged as open to Ukrainian workers are concentrated in hospitality, transport, manufacturing, food retail, restaurants, warehousing, and manual or operational roles. Their regional distribution appears to reflect sectoral structure and refugee settlement geography more than overall labour-market tightness. In care and public-health training, Pracuj.pl captures only a narrow part of direct care demand, while BUR shows a growing but still small public-health training segment. This reinforces the need to interpret demand–supply comparisons carefully where either source has known coverage limitations.

For policymakers, the results support three priorities. First, strengthen the alignment of subsidised training with employer demand in management, digital, ICT, business, and transversal skills. Second, maintain targeted support for care, health, and inclusion-related training, while recognising that online vacancies understate demand in public and social services. Third, develop more granular labour-market intelligence systems that combine online vacancy data, training registries, administrative sources, and taxonomies such as ESCO and Lightcast. Such systems can help Poland move from retrospective monitoring toward faster, evidence-based skill policy.

Introduction

This report provides a data-driven assessment of skills demand and training supply in Poland, with a particular focus on the extent to which publicly visible training provision is aligned with employers’ needs. The analysis combines two large-scale sources of labour-market intelligence: online job postings from Pracuj.pl, used as a proxy for employer demand, and training-service listings from Baza Usług Rozwojowych (BUR), used as a proxy for the supply of structured upskilling and reskilling opportunities. By applying natural language processing methods to both datasets, the report translates unstructured vacancy and training descriptions into comparable skill categories.

The central objective of the report is not to estimate the total number of jobs or training participants in Poland, but to compare the composition of skills demanded by employers with the composition of skills offered through the training system. This distinction is important. Online vacancies capture a specific segment of labour demand, especially market-based and private-sector recruitment, while BUR reflects the supply of registered training services rather than actual enrolment or completion. Despite these limitations, both sources provide timely and granular evidence that can complement official labour-market statistics and support more responsive skills policies.

The report is organised around three analytical questions. First, what types of skills are currently demanded in the Polish labour market, and how does this demand vary across sectors and regions? Second, what skills are being supplied through BUR training services, and how has this provision evolved over time? Third, where are the main mismatches between employer demand and training supply, especially in areas that are strategically relevant for productivity, inclusion, and structural transformation?

A key contribution of the analysis is the use of standardised skill taxonomies, primarily ESCO, to make job-posting and training data comparable. This enables the report to move beyond broad occupational categories and examine the specific competences, knowledge fields, and transversal skills that appear in both demand and supply. Additional analysis focuses on selected policy-relevant domains, including digital skills, artificial intelligence, green skills, care-related work, public health training, and job opportunities explicitly open to Ukrainian workers.

The findings show that Poland’s skill ecosystem is characterised by both strengths and gaps. Employer demand is strongly oriented toward management, communication, collaboration, digital, ICT, and business-related skills. Training supply, by contrast, places relatively greater emphasis on care, services, health, welfare, and machinery-related skills. This does not imply that these areas are overfunded or unimportant; many are linked to major demographic and social challenges. However, it does suggest that the current training portfolio may not fully reflect the structure of market-based employer demand, particularly in areas linked to digitalisation, organisational capabilities, and productivity growth.

The report also highlights the importance of interpreting data sources carefully. Pracuj.pl vacancies provide rich and timely information on employer demand, but they underrepresent some public-sector, informal, low-wage, and locally recruited jobs. BUR data offer valuable insights into training provision, but they do not measure training quality, take-up, completion, or labour-market outcomes. Therefore, the results should be read as evidence on the structure and direction of demand and supply, rather than as a definitive measure of aggregate labour-market shortages.

For policymakers, the report points to the value of building an integrated labour-market intelligence system that combines online vacancy data, training registries, administrative sources, and standardised skills taxonomies. Such a system could help identify emerging skill needs earlier, monitor whether training provision is adapting to structural change, and guide public investment in skills toward areas with the highest economic and social returns. In the Polish context, this is particularly relevant for digital transformation, the green transition, demographic ageing, migrant integration, and regional development.

Data Coverage

Data collection

We collect job advertisements from Pracuj.pl, the largest online job portal in Poland, and training-service listings from Baza Usług Rozwojowych, the country’s main public database of training and upskilling services. The analytical sample shown in this report focuses on records that can be assigned to Polish voivodeships and linked to the regional demand and supply comparison.

For job advertisements, we retain records with sufficient textual content to support downstream NLP processing, including job titles and descriptions. For BUR, we use training-service records with usable regional metadata and service descriptions. We remove duplicates and standardize core fields before the records enter the analytical pipeline.

Quantifying demand and supply

Estimating vacancies from job postings (OJV vs OJP)

  • Postings with an explicit vacancy count (6.7%) → taken at face value
  • Postings stating “multiple” positions without a number (8.9%) → coded as 2 vacancies (conservative)
  • Single-position postings (84.4%) → coded as 1 vacancy

Training data — scope and limitations

  • Training records include only minimum and maximum capacity per service — actual participant numbers are unavailable
  • Without attendance distributions, estimating total participants is not feasible
  • Analysis therefore focuses on the structure of training offerings: course types and skills taught

Skills are extracted from learning outcomes and service descriptions and mapped to ESCO.

Both sides are reduced to the same unit — the share of each skill group in demand vs. in supply. Skill analyses focus on composition, not on scaling postings to vacancies or courses to participants. What matters is that skill shares are measured consistently on both sides.

Why Pracuj.pl as the single source for online vacancies

Online job-posting research faces a methodological trade-off: (a) a single dominant portal with known sectoral selection bias, vs. (b) multi-source aggregation with noise from imperfect cross-source deduplication.

Cross-source deduplication is the core technical challenge in (b). The same vacancy may appear with slightly different titles, descriptions, or layouts across portals; identifying matches requires a similarity threshold that inevitably either over-merges (losing real vacancies) or under-merges (inflating counts).

Empirical context: Lightcast reports ~2.24M Polish postings in 2025 vs. ~731k unique postings on Pracuj.pl alone. Broader coverage explains part of the gap, but a 3× ratio is hard to reconcile with unique vacancies — likely reflecting residual duplicates.

This report uses a single-source approach based on Pracuj.pl — Poland’s largest commercial job portal, with strong coverage of white-collar, IT, and specialist roles. We do not claim full-population coverage of online vacancies; Pracuj.pl is treated as a high-quality, internally consistent sample of market labour demand.

Figure 5. Pracuj.pl estimated vacancies (flow) vs GUS open vacancies (stock), 2025

Interpretation. The comparison illustrates that Pracuj.pl and GUS measure different labour-market concepts: online posting flows versus end-of-quarter vacancy stocks. The two sources are complementary rather than substitutes.

Pracuj.pl flow series uses the conservative vacancy estimator described above. GUS figures refer to vacant jobs at the end of each quarter (stock). The two measures are complementary rather than directly comparable.

Source representativeness: Pracuj.pl vs MRPiPS / PUP

Pracuj.pl provides a conservative lower bound on online vacancies. The vacancy estimator codes empty fields as one position, explicit counts at face value, and “multiple positions” without a number as two.

MRPiPS administrative data capture vacancies reported by employers to poviat labour offices (PUP). The two sources reflect different market segments, not different measurements of the same population:

  • Pracuj.pl dominates white-collar, IT, and specialist hiring.
  • PUP reporting over-represents blue-collar, public-sector, and foreign-worker vacancies; private employers have no general obligation to report online vacancies to PUP.

Pracuj.pl is therefore treated as a strong proxy for market-driven labour demand. A seasonal drop in PUP vacancies from H1 to H2 may partly reflect cyclical hiring and activation programmes concentrated in the first half of the year.

Figure 6. Vacancy structure by KZiS major group: Pracuj.pl vs MRPiPS / PUP (2025, share of total)

Interpretation. The figure highlights selection differences between private online recruitment and public labour-office reporting. Pracuj.pl better captures market-driven, white-collar and specialist hiring, while PUP data better captures public-sector, blue-collar, and some foreign-worker vacancies.

Source: Pracuj.pl job postings mapped to KZiS via title embedding; MRPiPS / PUP vacancy reports for H1 and H2 2025 (MPRiPS).

Baza Usług Rozwojowych (BUR)

BUR is Poland’s largest national registry of training and advisory services, launched in 2016 under the EU Partnership Agreement and operated by PARP. The analysis is restricted to training services (Usługa szkoleniowa).

The registry includes diverse provider types — private companies, NGOs, public educational institutions, and public-finance entities — and, as of April 2025, 75% of registered providers offered services with public co-financing. From January 2026, registration in BUR is a mandatory prerequisite for providers delivering publicly funded training (EU funds and the National Training Fund).

Analytical scope. Skill-mismatch analysis compares 2025 BUR listings with 2025 job postings. Earlier BUR years are retained separately to trace how subsidised supply — for example in care services — evolved over funding cycles.

The full database contains ~870k training-service editions (2016–2025) and ~131k in 2025. Annual volumes reflect EU funding cycles (2014–2020 vs 2021–2027), pandemic disruption, and the system’s early ramp-up — not training needs alone. Analyses therefore work with within-year skill shares to reduce sensitivity to these volume swings.

Training providers in BUR (2025)

In 2025, roughly 3,100 providers delivered training through BUR — about half of all entities registered on the platform. Providers were classified by keywords in legal names (e.g. Sp. z o.o. / S.A. → private company; uniwersytet / politechnika → public education; fundacja / stowarzyszenie → NGO).

Course recurrence in BUR

BUR assigns a fresh id to every edition of a service, so raw posting counts cannot reveal whether the catalogue is genuinely new each year.

Strict “same course” key. Two postings are treated as the same course only if they share all four attributes: provider_id, normalised title (lowercased, diacritics stripped, edition/format markers removed), rounded number of hours, and kategoria_uslugi. A course is recurring if its key appears in ≥2 calendar years (2016–2025).

Figure 8. BUR postings by number of years a course remained on offer (2016–2025)

Interpretation. A substantial share of BUR postings are recurring offerings rather than entirely new courses. This points to stability in the training catalogue, but also raises questions about how quickly provision adapts to emerging skill demand.

Posting (edition): one BUR row — a single edition with its own date, location, and price. Course: editions sharing provider, normalised title, hours, and category. Recurring course: a course appearing in ≥2 calendar years.

Recognised qualifications in BUR (until 2023)

Until 2023, BUR distinguished four types of recognised qualifications in the inne_kwalifikacje questionnaire:

  • Q1 — vocational qualification (craftsman / master / KKZ)
  • Q2 — state or public-authority qualification (e.g. UDT, Welding Institute)
  • Q3 — position-based entitlement after validation (e.g. excavator operator)
  • Q4 — international certificate from an identified list

From 2024, the form structure changed; Q1–Q4 fields are no longer populated in the same way. The chart below shows the historical composition through 2023.

Figure 9. Share of BUR trainings ending with each recognised-qualification type (2016–2023)

Interpretation. Historically, recognised qualifications in BUR were distributed across several formal categories. Because the questionnaire changed after 2023, the figure is best used to understand the earlier qualification regime rather than current certification patterns.

Training completion documents (2025)

In 2025, BUR records whether a training ends with a formal competence certificate based on learning outcomes (Q17–Q19):

  • Q17 — document contains a description of learning outcomes
  • Q18 — validation carried out against criteria defined in learning outcomes
  • Q19 — separation of the training process from the validation process

A training is classified as ending with a recognised competence certificate only when all three conditions are met.

Figure 10. Type of document issued by BUR trainings (2025)

Interpretation. Most trainings with parsable metadata end with a recognised competence certificate. This indicates that BUR provision is often linked to formalised learning outcomes, although certificate quality and labour-market recognition may still vary.

In 2025, 77.5% of training services with parsable qualification metadata end with a recognised competence certificate (Q17–Q19); the remainder issue an informal or attendance certificate only.

Interpretation. The modality structure shows how far BUR provision has moved beyond purely classroom-based delivery. The balance between in-person, online, and hybrid formats matters for access, especially for workers outside major urban centres.

Training duration in BUR

Duration is recorded as liczba_godzin (contact hours) for each training-service edition. The analysis covers Usługa szkoleniowa records with positive hour values.

Median duration has remained in the low tens of hours over the registry’s lifetime, with a long right tail driven by formal qualifications, language courses, and degree-linked programmes. The 2025 distribution is strongly concentrated in short courses (≤40 h), while a minority of listings exceed 160 h — often multi-module certificates or study programmes registered on the platform.

Figure 12. BUR training duration — median, mean and 90th percentile by year

Interpretation. Training duration is typically short to medium, but the gap between the mean and upper percentiles indicates a long tail of more intensive programmes. This suggests that BUR mainly supports modular upskilling, with a smaller segment of longer qualification-oriented courses.

Source: BUR yearly exports (`Usługa szkoleniowa`, positive liczba_godzin).

Duration distribution and category profiles (2025)

In 2025, the median training length is 26 hours and the 90th percentile is 82 hours. Most subsidised services are designed as short upskilling modules rather than full qualification pathways, though a long tail of multi-module programmes remains.

Category medians vary widely: language and IT courses tend to be longer and more variable, while occupational safety (BHP) and soft-skills modules cluster at the short end.

Figure 13. Share of BUR trainings by duration bucket (2025)

Interpretation. The 2025 distribution confirms that most BUR training is delivered as relatively short courses. For policy, this means BUR is well suited for targeted upskilling but may be less suited, by itself, for deeper occupational transitions.

Figure 14. Median duration by BUR service category — top 10 by volume (2025)

Interpretation. Differences across categories show that training intensity varies substantially by field. Longer IT and language courses likely reflect higher learning requirements, while shorter safety and soft-skill courses reflect more standardised, modular provision.

Source: BUR 2025; categories with the largest number of training-service editions.

Key regional patterns

Geocoding and regional assignment

Job postings and BUR training services are assigned to Polish NUTS-2 voivodeships (and, where possible, powiat level) using a multi-step geocoding pipeline:

  1. Structured location fields — city and voivodeship names from the portal or BUR registry are normalised and matched against the official TERYT / SIMC register.
  2. Address geocoding — when powiat cannot be resolved from TERYT alone, the GUGiK UUG (Usługa Ujednoliconego Geokodowania) address API resolves city–voivodeship pairs to gmina and powiat codes.
  3. Regional aggregation — counts are summed to voivodeship level for the interactive maps and comparison table. Per-100k labour force normalisation uses GUS BDL average economically active population in 2025 as the denominator, enabling direct comparison of posting intensity and subsidised training supply across regions of different size.

Roughly 95% of Pracuj.pl postings with a usable location field resolve to a Polish powiat; the remainder are excluded from powiat-level views but retained in national aggregates. BUR records use provider or service location metadata with the same regional crosswalk.

Foreign or ambiguous locations are flagged and excluded from regional maps but included in national skill-mix statistics.

Change in BUR training supply (2019 vs 2025)

The map in Regional Coverage compares levels of training intensity in 2025. The chart below shows how subsidised training volumes shifted between 2019 and 2025 within each voivodeship — a period spanning two EU programming cycles and the post-pandemic recovery of BUR listings.

Red bars indicate voivodeships where the number of registered training-service editions declined; green bars indicate growth. The pattern reflects both funding-cycle effects and structural changes in how providers re-list courses on the platform, not labour-demand shifts alone.

Figure 2a. Percentage change in BUR training services by voivodeship (2019 → 2025)

Interpretation. Regional changes in BUR supply are uneven and should be interpreted cautiously. They likely reflect funding-cycle effects and provider re-listing practices as much as changes in local skill needs.

Source: BUR yearly exports (Usługa szkoleniowa), counted by provider-reported voivodeship.

Methodology

Processing pipeline

Raw job postings and training descriptions contain noisy, unstructured information in Polish (and occasionally English or other languages). We transform them into a standardised analytic dataset in six steps: we first identify the source language, translate non-Polish text into Polish, isolate skill-relevant sentences, map extracted skills to the ESCO and Lightcast skill taxonomies, standardise job titles to ESCO occupations using both titles and skill context for disambiguation, and then enrich each record with sector codes and regional information for voivodeship-level comparison.

Language
Detection
Language identification for each posting, including mixed-language offers
02
Translation
Gemma 3 Translate 4B converts non-Polish titles and descriptions into Polish
03
Skill-Sentence
Filtering
Fine-tuned BERT-architecture classifier identifies skill-relevant sentences
04
ESCO
Mapping
Custom contrastive bi-encoder maps skill sentences to ESCO skill entries
05
Job Title
Standardisation
Job titles are mapped to ESCO occupations using titles and extracted skills as context for disambiguation
06
Data
Augmentation
ISIC/NACE economic activity is assigned using the official ESCO-NACE crosswalk and job-ad context for disambiguation

Results

Skills Mismatch

What we compare

  • Demand side — every ESCO skill mention extracted from Pracuj.pl 2025 postings → 5.36 M mentions across ~731k offers
  • Supply side — every BUR training service mapped to ESCO via semantic matching → 719,265 trainings, 410,868 (training, ESCO-skill) tags

How we measure mismatch

Both sides share the same ESCO concept hierarchy (L1: 25 main groups · L2: 205 sub-groups). For each group g:

  • demand_share[g] = mentions[g] / Σ mentions
  • supply_share[g] = training_tags[g] / Σ training_tags
  • gap_pp[g] = (demand_share − supply_share) × 100 (percentage points)

How to read the result

  • Gap > 0 → under-supplied: employers request the skill more often than the training system delivers it
  • Gap < 0 → over-supplied: training output exceeds the demand signal from online vacancies

Why shares, not counts

Both sides are multi-tag (one offer can mention many skills; one training can teach many skills). Comparing tag shares is scale-free and robust to the absolute volume gap between online vacancies and subsidised training listings.

Caveats

Online vacancies under-represent public-sector and manual occupations, where BUR is most active — the measured over-supply for personal-care and protective-service skills is partly a demand-side blind spot. BUR captures only the subsidised and registered slice of training supply; commercial and in-house training is absent from the supply side. We test how much these and other measurement choices affect the results in the diagnostic cards at the end of this section.

Distribution of competences (all ESCO families)

Before drilling into skill pillars, the aggregate picture shows where tag mass concentrates on each side. ESCO skills (S1–S8) dominate demand mentions; knowledge concepts and transversal competences are also substantial. On the supply side, the S-pillar still leads, but knowledge and assisting & caring skills weigh more heavily than in vacancies — the first sign of compositional mismatch.

Figure 15. Share of ESCO tag mass by competence family — demand vs supply

Interpretation. The aggregate comparison shows the first clear sign of mismatch: demand is concentrated in skills, knowledge, and transversal competences, while supply places relatively more weight on care-related and knowledge areas.

Source: Pracuj.pl 2025 ESCO mentions vs BUR 2025 training tags.

Skill mix — demand vs supply (ESCO S1–S8)

Figure 16. ESCO skill mix on the demand and supply sides (S1–S8, share of tag mass)

Interpretation. Management, communication, digital, and ICT-related skills are more prominent in vacancies than in BUR training tags. Conversely, care, services, and machinery-related skills are more prominent in training supply.

Source: Pracuj.pl ESCO skill mentions vs BUR training tags, 2025.

Management skills (S4) account for 21.9% of demand-side mentions but only 8.1% of training tags — the largest positive gap in the catalogue. Communication / collaboration / creativity (S1) is the second-largest demand block (17.0%) and comparatively well covered (13.8%). Working with computers (S5) and ICT knowledge (06) show meaningful positive gaps — a digital-skills signal that the BUR mix has not fully caught up with. Conversely, Assisting & caring (S3), Working with machinery (S8) and Services (10) are the largest over-supplied groups — partly reflecting EU-funded reskilling priorities and partly online vacancies under-representing those occupations.

Poland in context: demand-side ESCO mix across countries

To anchor the Poland 2025 findings against international comparators, we re-use the country panel from the World Bank East Asia skill-demand report (mimeo).

The Poland demand mix (top row) sits next to the East Asia and benchmark panel. Communication, collaboration and creativity (S1) and management skills (S4) dominate everywhere, but their relative weight differs: Poland leans more on management (S4) than India or Indonesia, and is closer to Singapore and South Korea in the share of working with computers (S5). Assisting & caring (S3) is markedly lower on the demand side in Poland than in Southeast Asian benchmarks — consistent with the under-representation of care and public-sector hiring in Pracuj.pl noted in the caveats above. Bars sum to 100% of the S1–S8 family within each country.

Source: ESCO S1–S8 demand-side shares. Poland (highlighted) uses the figures from Figure 16 of this report; other countries come from the East Asia skill-demand report.

Where supply lags demand (gap in pp)

Figure 17. Demand–supply gap by ESCO skill pillar (S1–S8, percentage points)

Interpretation. The gap profile separates demand-heavy white-collar and digital skills from supply-heavy care, services, and machinery skills. The policy implication is a need to rebalance part of subsidised training toward business, management, digital, and transversal capabilities.

The chart is dominated by two forces: a white-collar / cognitive deficit on the demand-heavy side — management, digital, team-working and ICT knowledge — and a personal-services / blue-collar surplus on the supply-heavy side — assisting & caring, machinery, services, handling & moving. The deficit on the red side is concentrated in occupations where online vacancies provide near-complete coverage; the green side partly reflects measurement limits rather than genuine over-provision.

Top L2 sub-groups — under- and over-supplied

Figure 18. Most under-supplied L2 skill groups

Interpretation. The largest under-supplied sub-groups include management, business administration, teamwork, digital data access, and ICT knowledge. These are broad productivity-relevant skills that cut across many sectors.

Figure 19. Most over-supplied L2 skill groups

Interpretation. Over-supplied groups cluster around personal care, protective services, driving, and health-care delivery. This may partly reflect genuine policy priorities, but also the fact that Pracuj.pl under-represents some public and manual occupations.

Source: ESCO L2 groups; ranked by absolute gap in percentage points.

At L2, generic management skills (S4.0) alone show a +13 pp gap, followed by business & administration (041), collaborating in teams (T4.3), accessing digital data (S5.5) and ICT knowledge (061). The over-supplied panel clusters around personal care (S3.6), protective services (S3.3), driving (S8.2) and health-care delivery (S3.2) — aligning with EU-financed reskilling priorities and sectors where hiring migrates offline.

Transversal, knowledge and language competences

The S-pillar summary masks important gaps in transversal and knowledge domains. Employers overweight social & communication (T4) and self-management (T3) relative to BUR; training supply is thin on both. Among knowledge fields, business & administration (04) and ICT (06) are under-represented in training tags, while services (10) and health & welfare (09) are over-represented — mirroring the care and public-service bias of subsidised programmes.

Languages are shown on a renormalised within-pillar basis (top nine demand languages plus an “Other” bucket; Polish and generic L1 tags excluded), matching the standalone mismatch charts. English and German still dominate employer demand; training supply is spread across several languages rather than appearing only on the demand side at near-zero global shares.

Figure 20. Transversal competences (T1–T6): demand vs supply shares within the transversal pillar (each side renormalised to 100%)

Interpretation. Employers place relatively more weight on social, communication, and self-management competences than the BUR training mix does. These transversal gaps matter because such skills are valuable across occupations and sectors.

Figure 21. Knowledge fields (ISCED-F): demand vs supply shares within the knowledge pillar (each side renormalised to 100%)

Interpretation. Business, administration, and ICT knowledge appear under-represented in training relative to demand, while services and health-related knowledge are more prominent in supply. This reinforces the broader mismatch between market hiring and subsidised provision.

Figure 22. Languages: demand vs supply shares within the language pillar (Polish excluded; long tail grouped as Other; each side renormalised to 100%)

Interpretation. English and German dominate language demand, while training supply appears more diversified across languages. For employability policy, language training should remain demand-sensitive rather than evenly distributed across language categories.

Measuring overall mismatch: Jensen–Shannon divergence

Treating skill shares as probability distributions, we summarise overall compositional distance with the Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD). Values lie in [0, 1] (base 2): 0 means identical mixes; values around 0.16 indicate a moderate L1 (S1–S8) mismatch; ~0.30 at L2 signals a substantial reallocation need within skill sub-groups.

JSD compares renormalised S-pillar distributions on the demand and supply sides. L1 JSD ≈ 0.16; L2 JSD ≈ 0.30 (2025, Pracuj.pl vs BUR).

Interpretation. The JSD indicator summarises the overall distance between demand and supply skill distributions. The reported values suggest moderate mismatch at the broad skill-pillar level and more substantial mismatch at the detailed sub-group level.

Are the mismatch results stable?

The figures above rest on two non-trivial modelling choices: how each posting and training is weighted into the aggregate shares, and which slice of the labour market the Pracuj.pl sample actually represents. Before drawing policy conclusions we need to know whether the headline gap survives plausible alternative choices. The two cards below answer that question. They are not new results — they are stress tests of the results above. Each one states why we are worried, what we compute, and what we conclude.

Sensitivity — does posting verbosity drive the picture?

Why we worry

A senior CTO posting can list 20 ESCO skill mentions; a 1-line warehouse-worker posting can list 1. Under the headline weighting scheme (“mention-mass”) that CTO posting carries 20× more weight in the demand shares than the warehouse posting. If ICT and management-heavy postings are systematically more verbose than care-work postings, the white-collar deficit could be partly an artefact of how many tags get written into a job description, not of how many jobs are open.

What we compute

We rebuild the demand- and supply-side share vectors under a second weighting scheme — per-posting — where each posting (or each training) contributes exactly one unit of weight, distributed evenly across the skills it mentions:

  • mention-mass (headline): \(s_g^{MM} = \dfrac{\sum_i \mathrm{count}_i(g)}{\sum_i |S_i|}\)
  • per-posting (alternative): \(s_g^{PP} = \dfrac{1}{N} \sum_i \dfrac{\mathrm{count}_i(g)}{|S_i|}\)

Then we compare the two vectors on each side and — more importantly — on the gap (demand − supply) that actually drives every chart above.

What we find

Comparison L1 distance Cosine similarity Max single-group shift
Demand: MM vs PP 0.061 0.998 0.81 pp (ICT, code 06)
Supply: MM vs PP 0.034 0.9996 0.52 pp (generic language placeholder)

And on the gap vector itself (54 ESCO L1 groups):

  • Pearson r between MM- and PP-derived gaps: 0.998
  • max |Δ gap_pp| across all groups: 0.81 pp
  • top-10 under-supplied groups: 10 / 10 overlap between the two schemes
  • top-10 over-supplied groups: 9 / 10 overlap

Verdict. ICT-heavy postings do list more ESCO tags than the average posting, so the per-posting scheme shaves ~0.8 pp off ICT’s demand share. But no top-ranked under-supplied group moves and no single group’s share shifts by more than ~1 pp. The headline narrative — large positive gap on management (S4), positive gap on digital (S5) and ICT knowledge (06), negative gap on assisting & caring (S3) and working with machinery (S8) — holds verbatim. Verbosity is not driving the picture. We keep mention-mass as the headline because it is the standard ESCO accounting unit and is comparable to other published ESCO mention-rate studies.

Robustness — does the Pracuj.pl sectoral skew drive the picture?

Why we worry

Pracuj.pl is a private-sector online job board. Some sectors are heavily over-represented relative to actual Polish employment — most strikingly Administrative and support services (NACE section N, which includes temp-work and recruiting agencies): 24.4 % of postings vs 2.75 % of employment, because agencies re-post vacancies that ultimately belong to other sectors. Conversely, agriculture (A), mining (B), education (P), human health (Q) and information & communication (J) are markedly under-represented in the OJP universe relative to LFS employment shares. A substantial part of the apparent skill mismatch could be a story about “who advertises on Pracuj” rather than “what Poland’s labour market demands”.

What we compute

Standard post-stratification. For each NACE section k we calculate a sectoral weight

\[ w_k \;=\; \frac{p_k^{\text{target}}}{p_k^{\text{pracuj}}} \]

where \(p_k^{\text{target}}\) is section k’s share of total Polish employment (Eurostat LFS 2024, ages 15+, both sexes — the international counterpart of the GUS BAEL/LFS series “Pracujący w gospodarce narodowej wg sekcji PKD”) and \(p_k^{\text{pracuj}}\) is its share in our Pracuj.pl analysis sample. Each posting in section k enters the aggregation with weight \(w_k\), and the demand-side ESCO L1 shares are recomputed on the weighted sample. Weights range from \(w_N \approx 0.11\) (administrative & support, heavily downweighted) to \(w_B \approx 15.4\) (mining, heavily upweighted); the median section keeps roughly its OJP weight.

What we find

This is the largest perturbation we apply to the demand vector:

Comparison Result
L1 distance (headline vs reweighted) 0.173
Cosine similarity 0.988
Largest single-group fall −2.10 pp for ICT knowledge (06)
Second-largest fall −1.88 pp for management (S4)
Largest single-group rise +1.51 pp for working with machinery (S8)

The biggest losers under reweighting are the white-collar / digital groups disproportionately mentioned by recruiting-agency, finance and real-estate postings. ICT knowledge (06) falls from 4.1 % to 2.0 %, management (S4) from 17.5 % to 15.6 %, business & administration (04) from 7.6 % to 6.2 %. The biggest winners are primary- and education-heavy groups: machinery (S8) rises from 3.6 % to 5.1 %, education knowledge (01) from 2.6 % to 3.7 %, agriculture/forestry/fisheries knowledge (A1) from 5.9 % to 6.5 %.

What about the mismatch — the demand-minus-supply gap that every figure above visualises?

  • Pearson r between headline and reweighted gap vectors: 0.985
  • max |Δ gap_pp| across all groups: 2.10 pp
  • top-10 under-supplied groups: 9 / 10 overlap
  • top-10 over-supplied groups: 9 / 10 overlap

Verdict. The directional conclusions hold across the board: large positive gap on management and business/administration; meaningful positive gap on transversal social skills; large negative gap on assisting & caring, machinery and services. The single substantive change is the digital-skills deficit (working with computers S5 + ICT knowledge 06): its magnitude is roughly halved once Pracuj is reweighted to Poland’s actual sectoral employment mix. That tells us roughly half of the headline digital gap is a true economy-wide demand-supply imbalance and roughly half is a composition effect of Pracuj over-sampling digital-intensive sectors. Both halves are still policy-relevant, but for different reasons — the first calls for adjusting subsidised training, the second for reading OJP-based digital-skill indicators with appropriate humility.

AI Skills Demand

The demand for AI-related skills is highly dynamic, with new technologies and tools emerging rapidly while others become obsolete. This makes it difficult to track AI skill demand using static taxonomies alone.

Lightcast captures highly granular and technology-specific signals, such as individual AI tools, models, copilots, libraries, and chatbot platforms. This makes it well suited to detecting early changes in employer demand. We start from a benchmark of 350 AI skills from Lightcast used by Martins-Neto et al. (2026) and extend it with 114 additional skills that have since appeared in the Lightcast taxonomy, bringing the current total to 464 AI skills.

To make the full list policy-readable, we organize these 464 skills into four primary categories and eight cross-cutting tags. The primary categories are mutually exclusive and capture the fundamental domain of each skill. The tags are non-exclusive and highlight secondary dimensions that cut across categories.

Source: Lightcast AI skills taxonomy; Martins-Neto et al. (2026); authors' categorization.

Green Skills Demand

Identification approach

Green skills are identified by matching the ESCO skills extracted from job postings (Step 04 of the pipeline) against the official ESCO Green Skills and Knowledge Collection↗, a curated subset of roughly 830 skills and knowledge concepts that the European Commission classifies as relevant to the green transition.

A job posting is counted as “green” if at least one of its matched ESCO skills belongs to this collection. Because the ESCO green taxonomy is broad and includes some entries that are only tangentially related to environmental sustainability, we apply a manual review step: each matched skill is classified as either genuine green or false positive based on whether its presence in a job posting plausibly signals demand for environmental or sustainability competences.

False positives

Not all skills in the ESCO green collection carry a clear environmental signal when they appear in Polish job postings. Skills such as building codes, vehicle type-approval, or warehouse management software are part of the ESCO green taxonomy but frequently appear in postings where the role has no meaningful green dimension. After matching, we manually flag these as false positives and exclude them from the headline green skill counts. The full list of excluded skills is shown below.

Show excluded false-positive skills (click to expand)

The map shows the share of job postings with at least one genuine green skill in each voivodeship. Regional variation is moderate: shares range from roughly 2.5% to 4.0%, with higher concentrations in voivodeships where construction, energy, and agricultural sectors are more prominent.

Figure 31a. Share of job postings with at least one green skill, by voivodeship

Interpretation. Green-skill demand varies moderately across regions, with higher shares in areas linked to construction, energy, and agriculture. Regional green policies should therefore account for local industrial structure.

Source: Pracuj.pl job postings; ESCO Green Skills Collection; authors' matching and manual review.

Interpretation. The leading green skills are linked to environmental engineering, environmental management, and heating/cooling systems. This points to practical green-transition demand in construction, energy infrastructure, and environmental compliance.

Interpretation. Green intensity is highest in utilities, energy, agriculture, and public administration, where regulation and sustainability obligations are salient. However, large sectors with lower intensity may still generate substantial absolute demand.

The most common green skills for this occupation include promoting sustainability, advising on the energy efficiency of heating systems, installing photovoltaic systems, energy efficiency, agronomy, and the energy performance of buildings. Jobs for Ukrainians

Background

Polish job postings on Pracuj.pl can carry an explicit Запрошуємо працівників з України / Jobs for Ukrainians badge, added by the employer to signal that the role is open to (and the workplace is prepared to support) Ukrainian candidates. The tag was introduced shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 as part of Pracuj.pl’s response to the wave of refugees arriving in Poland — see Grupa Pracuj dla Ukrainy↗.

We retrieve the badge by parsing the data-test="sections-benefit-ukrainian-friendly" HTML element on each posting’s detail page, and join the result back to the structured fields in job_ads. Looking at where this tag appears tells us which regions, industries and occupations are most actively opening up to workers from Ukraine — and by extension, to foreign labour more broadly. It also reveals where employer demand and refugee supply overlap most strongly.

Regional intensity

The map shows the share of all 2025 Pracuj.pl postings in each voivodeship that carry the Jobs-for-Ukrainians tag. Małopolskie leads clearly (around 14% of postings), followed by Lubuskie, Łódzkie, Lubelskie and Dolnośląskie — a mix of regions with large refugee populations (Małopolskie, Dolnośląskie), border-area logistics hubs and food-processing clusters (Lubuskie, Lubelskie, Łódzkie). Mazowieckie has the largest absolute number of tagged offers but a lower share, since its labour market is dominated by professional and IT roles where the tag is less commonly used.

Figure 34a. Share of postings tagged 'Jobs for Ukrainians', by voivodeship (2025)

Interpretation. Ukrainian-friendly postings are regionally uneven, with Małopolskie standing out. The pattern likely reflects refugee settlement geography and sectoral composition rather than general labour-market tightness alone.

Source: Pracuj.pl postings with data-test="sections-benefit-ukrainian-friendly"; authors' parsing.

Demand intensity vs Ukrainian-friendly share

A natural question is whether voivodeships with a hotter labour market — measured as total job offers per 100k labour force — are also the ones where employers more often choose to flag a posting as Ukrainian-friendly. Plotting the within-region share (Y, %) against total offer intensity (X) gives a much weaker relationship than one might expect: across the 16 voivodeships, Pearson r ≈ +0.24, Spearman ρ ≈ +0.26, R² ≈ 0.06. In other words, demand intensity explains very little of the cross-regional variation in how often the badge is used.

The clearest outlier is Małopolskie, sitting well above the cloud at ≈14% of postings tagged despite only mid-range overall intensity — a likely echo of Kraków’s large post-2022 Ukrainian diaspora. Kujawsko-Pomorskie (~6.6%) and Podkarpackie (~7.0%) sit clearly below the cloud, while Mazowieckie — by far the densest labour market — is exactly average on the share dimension (~9.7%). This suggests the Ukrainian-friendly tag tracks demographic factors (refugee settlement patterns) and sectoral mix much more than overall hiring intensity.

Figure 34b. Total offers per 100k labour force vs share of offers tagged 'Jobs for Ukrainians', by voivodeship

Interpretation. The weak relationship between overall demand intensity and Ukrainian-friendly shares suggests that employers’ openness to Ukrainian workers is driven more by sectoral and demographic factors than by aggregate vacancy pressure.

Source: Pracuj.pl postings; Statistics Poland (BAEL) labour-force averages 2025; authors' computation. Each marker is one of the 16 voivodeships; the dashed line is the OLS fit.

Beyond the voivodeship map — decomposing where the tag really comes from

The voivodeship picture above is suggestive but limited. An aggregate map cannot tell whether a local gap in Ukrainian-friendly hiring is driven by what employers hire for (sectoral mix) or how they hire within those sectors (behaviour). To answer this we apply a shift-share (Oaxaca) decomposition on 683,104 postings with a resolved powiat and a NACE mapping.

Shift-share (Oaxaca) decomposition

For every powiat \(p\), the deviation of its Ukrainian-friendly share from the national share can be written exactly as

\[ s_p - s_{PL} \;=\; \underbrace{\sum_k w_{pk}\bigl(s_{pk} - s_{PL,k}\bigr)}_{\text{within-sector (behavioural)}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_k \bigl(w_{pk}-w_{PL,k}\bigr) s_{PL,k}}_{\text{between-sector (composition)}} \]

where \(k\) indexes NACE divisions (2-digit codes), \(w_{pk}\) is the share of postings in division \(k\) within powiat \(p\), and \(s_{pk}\) is the local within-division Ukrainian-friendly share. The first term answers: “Given the sectors that operate here, how much more (or less) often does an employer flag the tag than the national norm?” The second answers: “How much of the gap is just due to over- or under- representation of UA-friendly-prone sectors?”

Figure 34c. Shift-share decomposition of the Ukrainian-friendly gap from the national share — 16 voivodeships

Interpretation. Małopolskie's +4.8 pp gap is almost entirely behavioural — its sectoral mix accounts for just +0.2 pp; the rest is local employers being more willing to flag the tag. The reverse is true for Mazowieckie, where a slightly positive within-sector signal is dragged below zero by an over-representation of professional / IT roles where the tag is rarely used.

Source: Pracuj.pl postings (2025); NACE division mapping; authors' computation. Diamonds mark the observed gap = within + between.

Figure 34d. Shift-share decomposition — top-20 powiats by |gap|

Interpretation. Polkowicki's +20.8 pp gap is dominated by the within-sector term (+19.6 pp): even at the same sectoral mix as Poland, local employers there flag the tag far more often. Tatrzański is the clearest "composition" case — about a third of its gap is a hospitality-and-services tilt typical of mountain resorts.

Source: Pracuj.pl postings (2025). Only powiats with ≥ 100 postings are eligible; ranking by absolute gap.

Industries (NACE sections)

Aggregated to the top-level NACE section, the Ukrainian-friendly tag is strongly concentrated in service sectors that absorb low-barrier labour: accommodation and food service (I) stands out at roughly a third of all postings, followed by transportation and storage (H) and manufacturing (C). Sections dominated by professional services and public administration use the tag much less frequently.

Figure 34e. NACE sections with the highest share of Ukrainian-friendly postings

Interpretation. Ukrainian-friendly hiring is concentrated in hospitality, transport, and manufacturing. These sectors often involve operational roles with lower formal credential barriers and higher labour turnover.

Source: Pracuj.pl + ESCO→NACE crosswalk. Sections shown have at least 5,000 postings.

Industries (NACE divisions)

Drilling down to NACE divisions exposes the specific niches driving demand for Ukrainian workers. By share, the leaders are food retail and restaurants (G47.5, G47.22, I56.11, G47.11), passenger road transport (H49.32, H49.33) and goods road transport (H49.41) — sectors with high turnover, language-tolerant tasks and a strong refugee employment footprint. By absolute volume, restaurants (I56.11), warehousing (H52.1) and programming activities (K62.1) dominate, the last reflecting the large pool of Ukrainian IT specialists who relocated after 2022.

Figure 34f. NACE divisions with the highest share of Ukrainian-friendly postings

Interpretation. At a more detailed sector level, food retail, restaurants, and road transport stand out. These niches are particularly important for refugee and migrant labour-market integration.

Figure 34g. NACE divisions with the largest absolute number of Ukrainian-friendly postings

Interpretation. In absolute terms, restaurants, warehousing, and programming activities dominate Ukrainian-friendly postings. This shows that both lower-barrier service work and higher-skill IT employment matter for Ukrainian workers in Poland.

Source: Pracuj.pl + ESCO→NACE crosswalk. Only divisions with at least 500 postings are ranked.

Occupational categories

Using Pracuj.pl’s own narrow job categories (job_category_narrow), the tag is most prevalent in food-related and manual-labour roles — Food products, Hospitality staff, Manual labour, Couriers / delivery — and in hospitality and personal-services categories such as Hotel operations and Hairdresser / beautician. The absolute-volume ranking confirms that gastronomy, courier and warehouse categories together account for the bulk of Ukrainian-friendly hiring.

Figure 34h. Narrow job categories with the highest share of Ukrainian-friendly postings

Interpretation. The tag is most prevalent in food-related, hospitality, manual-labour, courier, and personal-service categories. These are practical entry points for migrant employment policy.

Figure 34i. Narrow job categories with the largest absolute number of Ukrainian-friendly postings

Interpretation. High-volume Ukrainian-friendly hiring is concentrated in gastronomy, courier, warehouse, and related operational categories. This identifies where language support, credential recognition, and workplace integration could have the largest reach.

Source: Pracuj.pl job_category_narrow. Only categories with at least 500 postings are ranked.

NACE sectors — Ukrainian-friendly vs other postings

The Ukrainian-friendly tag is unevenly distributed across the economy. Transport (H), hospitality (I) and manufacturing (C) show the largest positive gaps versus other postings — consistent with operational hiring in logistics, food service and plant work. Professional services (N) and finance (L) under-index sharply, reflecting credential and language barriers in those segments.

Figure 34j. Over- and under-representation of NACE sections among Ukrainian-friendly postings

Bar = percentage-point gap between the share of postings within each segment. Sections below 0.2% in both segments are omitted.

Interpretation. Transport, hospitality, and manufacturing over-index among Ukrainian-friendly postings, while professional services and finance under-index. This reflects both language and credential barriers and the occupational composition of migrant-accessible jobs.

Source: Pracuj.pl 2025; occupation → NACE crosswalk. Right-hand labels show within-segment shares for UA-tagged vs other postings.

Seniority and contract types

The tag overwhelmingly attaches to manual-worker roles — over a fifth of such postings are Ukrainian-friendly — and to a hybrid manager / supervisor shift-leader category common in retail and gastronomy. Specialist, expert and director roles see the tag much less. On the contract side, temporary employment contracts and contracts of mandate carry the tag most often, reflecting the prevalence of short-tenure agency-style hiring in the segments where Ukrainian workers are most actively recruited; standard permanent contracts and B2B contracts use the tag considerably less.

Figure 34k. Share of postings tagged 'Jobs for Ukrainians', by seniority level

Interpretation. Ukrainian-friendly postings are concentrated in manual-worker and supervisor-type roles, while specialist and director roles use the tag less often. This suggests that the badge mainly supports operational rather than high-skill professional recruitment.

Figure 34l. Share of postings tagged 'Jobs for Ukrainians', by contract type

Interpretation. Temporary and mandate contracts carry the tag more often than permanent or B2B contracts. This points to a relatively flexible and sometimes more precarious employment structure in migrant-accessible segments.

Source: Pracuj.pl seniority_level and contract_types. Multi-valued fields are split per posting; only categories with at least 500 postings are shown.

Care Services and Public Health Training

Demand for care services in online vacancies

Using KZiS-aligned occupation codes (care and social-work families), we identify ~1,100 postings in 2025 that signal direct care-service delivery — a narrow slice of Pracuj.pl dominated by medical care assistants, elderly-care workers and related roles. A broader text-and-title classifier surfaces roughly 14,200 postings when clinical and therapeutic occupations are included.

Employer concentration is high in both segments: the top 10 employers account for roughly half of care-tagged offers, compared with a more fragmented market in general healthcare NACE postings.

Figure 35. Top care-related occupations by posting volume (KZiS-mapped titles, 2025)

Interpretation. Direct care demand captured by Pracuj.pl is small and concentrated in a limited set of occupations. This likely understates broader care-sector demand, especially in public and municipal services.

Source: Pracuj.pl 2025; KZiS-mapped occupation titles.

Skills profile of care-related offers

Care postings emphasise assisting & caring (S3) and management (S4) more than the general healthcare NACE sample, while ICT (S5) is less prominent — reflecting hands-on and coordination tasks rather than hospital IT roles. Top requested skills include computer literacy, management skills and elderly care; knowledge demand centres on paramedical practice and nursing science.

Figure 36. Top ESCO skills in care-related offers

Interpretation. Care-related postings combine hands-on care skills with general digital and management skills. This suggests that even direct care roles increasingly require coordination and basic administrative capabilities.

Figure 37. Top knowledge concepts in care-related offers

Interpretation. Knowledge demand in care postings centres on paramedical practice and nursing-related knowledge. This confirms that care work often requires occupation-specific knowledge, not only generic empathy or assistance skills.

Figure 38. Care services vs NACE R86 healthcare — share of offers with each S-pillar skill

Interpretation. Care-service postings differ from the broader healthcare sector by placing more emphasis on assisting, caring, and management skills and less on ICT. This helps distinguish direct care roles from the wider healthcare labour market.

Source: Pracuj.pl ESCO skill mentions, 2025.

Public-health training in BUR

BUR listings classified as public health / medical professions remain a small share of the registry (0.89% in 2025, 1,165 services) but have grown sharply since 2022. Training is overwhelmingly in-person (~87%) and short to medium length (median bucket 9–16 h and 25–40 h). Regional supply is led by Śląskie, Pomorskie and Małopolskie.

Within this subset, ESCO tags stress assisting & caring (S3) — nursing, patient care and rehabilitation — with supporting shares for communication (S1) and information skills (S2). Top training skills include elderly care, first aid and podiatry consultations.

Figure 39. Public-health BUR trainings as share of all BUR services (2016–2025)

Interpretation. Public-health training remains a small share of BUR but has grown since 2022. This suggests rising policy and provider attention, though the scale remains limited relative to the full training catalogue.

Figure 40. ESCO skill-pillar mix in public-health BUR trainings (2025)

Interpretation. Public-health BUR training is strongly oriented toward assisting and caring skills, with additional communication and information skills. This profile is consistent with practical service-delivery training.

Figure 41. Top voivodeships for public-health BUR training services

Interpretation. Public-health training supply is regionally concentrated, led by Śląskie, Pomorskie, and Małopolskie. Regional concentration may reflect provider location, funding availability, or local health-sector demand.

Figure 42. Delivery modality — public-health BUR (2025)

Interpretation. Public-health training is overwhelmingly in-person, reflecting the practical and hands-on nature of many care and health competences. This may limit access for workers in regions with fewer providers.

Figure 43. Duration distribution — public-health BUR (2025)

Interpretation. Public-health training is mostly short to medium length. This suggests a focus on modular competence development rather than long formal qualification pathways.

Figure 44. Top skills taught in public-health BUR trainings

Interpretation. The leading skills taught include elderly care, first aid, rehabilitation, and related practical care competences. These align with ageing-related service needs and the operational requirements of care delivery.

Source: BUR 2016–2025; public-health subset via service category and keyword rules.

The demand–supply comparison for care skills should be read alongside the skills-mismatch caveats: Pracuj.pl under-represents public hospitals and municipal social care, while BUR over-indexes subsidised care reskilling — so apparent over-supply of assisting & caring skills partly reflects complementary coverage of the two data sources.

Conclusions

This report demonstrates that online labour-market intelligence can provide a timely and granular view of Poland’s evolving skills landscape. By combining vacancy data from Pracuj.pl with training-service data from Baza Usług Rozwojowych (BUR), the analysis offers a structured comparison between the skills employers request and the skills supplied through registered training provision. While neither source should be interpreted as a complete representation of the labour market or the training system, together they provide valuable evidence on the direction of skills demand, the orientation of training supply, and potential areas of misalignment.

The findings suggest that Poland’s skills system faces a dual challenge. On the one hand, employers continue to demand a broad set of foundational and transversal skills, including communication, collaboration, management, self-organisation, and business-related competences. These skills are not confined to a single sector or occupation; rather, they underpin productivity across much of the economy. On the other hand, demand for more specialised skills linked to digitalisation, ICT, data use, artificial intelligence, and the green transition is becoming increasingly visible. This combination points to a labour market in which both general employability skills and more advanced technical capabilities are central to future competitiveness.

The comparison with BUR training provision shows that the current training offer only partly reflects this structure of demand. Training supply is relatively more concentrated in care, health, welfare, services, and machinery-related areas, while employer demand is more strongly oriented toward management, business administration, digital, ICT, communication, and teamwork-related skills. This does not mean that the areas emphasised in training supply are unimportant. Many of them respond to genuine social needs, including demographic ageing, health-care pressures, and demand for care-related services. However, the observed differences indicate that training policy may need to more explicitly balance social priorities with the skills required for productivity growth, organisational upgrading, and digital transformation.

Digital skills deserve particular attention. The analysis shows that employer demand is not limited to basic digital literacy. Advanced digital skills constitute a substantial share of classified digital-skill mentions, suggesting that many firms are already seeking capabilities related to data, software, ICT systems, and more complex digital tasks. At the same time, AI-related demand remains relatively concentrated in knowledge-intensive sectors, especially professional, scientific, technical, information, and communication activities. This pattern is consistent with an early stage of diffusion, where AI capabilities are not yet universal but are strategically important for high-productivity segments of the economy. Skills policy should therefore avoid treating AI as a niche technology while also recognising that broad-based AI adoption will require complementary managerial, organisational, and transversal skills.

Green skills show a different pattern. Their regional variation is moderate, but their sectoral concentration is clearer, with stronger intensity in utilities, energy-related activities, agriculture, public administration, and selected technical fields. At the same time, many green-skill mentions appear in larger sectors where the green share is lower but the absolute number of affected workers may be substantial. This distinction matters for policy design. Targeted sectoral interventions are needed in high-intensity green-transition sectors, while broader upskilling efforts should ensure that green competences also reach mainstream occupations in trade, manufacturing, construction, and professional services.

The report also points to the importance of inclusion-oriented skills policy. Job postings explicitly open to Ukrainian workers are concentrated in specific sectors and occupations, including hospitality, transport, manufacturing, warehousing, food services, and selected IT-related roles. This suggests that migrant integration policies should combine general labour-market access measures with sector-specific support, including language training, recognition of prior experience, workplace integration, and pathways from entry-level jobs toward more stable and higher-productivity employment. Similarly, the analysis of care-related work and public-health training highlights the need to interpret online vacancy data in relation to coverage patterns, as some socially important areas of labour demand may be less visible in private job boards than in other administrative or sector-specific sources.

A key methodological conclusion is that no single data source provides a complete view of skills demand and supply. The value of online labour-market data lies in its timeliness, granularity, and rich textual content, but also in the fact that it captures a particular segment of the labour market. In the Polish context, Pracuj.pl provides especially strong coverage of market-based recruitment for white-collar, specialist, managerial, and ICT-related occupations. Official vacancy registers and public employment service data, by contrast, tend to capture a different part of the labour market, including more blue-collar, lower-wage, public-sector, and locally recruited vacancies. These sources should therefore not be treated as competing measures of the same phenomenon, but as complementary windows into different segments of labour demand.

The same logic applies to the supply side. BUR data provide detailed and verified information on registered training services, but they represent only one part of the broader skills supply ecosystem. A fuller assessment of skills provision would require linking BUR data with additional sources, such as curricula from vocational and higher education institutions, adult-learning programmes, sectoral training initiatives, certification schemes, and employer-provided training. Integrating these sources would make it possible to compare not only the skills demanded by employers and advertised by training providers, but also the skills embedded in formal education pathways and other learning opportunities.

A promising next step is therefore to build a more integrated skills intelligence system that combines multiple verified sources with different coverage profiles. Such a system would use online job postings, official vacancy registers, public employment service data, training registries, curricula, and possibly stated preference studies as complementary evidence. Online and administrative data can reveal observed demand and available supply, while stated preference studies can help explain worker and employer choices, constraints, and willingness to participate in training. Together, these sources would provide a more balanced picture of Poland’s skills ecosystem and support better-targeted policy decisions.

For Poland, the results support a shift from static training planning toward a more adaptive skills system. Such a system would regularly compare employer demand with training supply, identify emerging skill gaps earlier, and provide evidence for reallocating public funding toward areas with strong economic and social returns. This does not imply that training provision should mechanically follow current vacancies. Public policy must also account for long-term development goals, demographic pressures, regional cohesion, and inclusion. However, systematic skills intelligence can help ensure that these priorities are pursued with a clearer understanding of labour-market needs.

Overall, the analysis suggests that Poland has a substantial opportunity to strengthen the alignment between its training ecosystem and the changing structure of work. Better alignment would require expanding provision in digital, ICT, business, management, and transversal skills, while preserving targeted support for care, health, green transition, and migrant integration.

Technical annex

NLP Processing Methods

This annex documents the natural-language-processing steps behind the skills measures used in the report. The main Methodology section shows the six-step pipeline; this annex explains what happens inside those steps and why the choices matter for interpretation.

Step 01 — Language Detection

Most Pracuj.pl postings are in Polish, but a non-trivial share contains English titles, English descriptions, or mixed-language text. We detect the language of both the title and the full description so that Polish text can pass through unchanged while non-Polish fields are routed to translation.

Language detection is applied per field rather than per posting because a common online-vacancy pattern is an English title with a Polish body, or the reverse. This avoids translating already-usable Polish text and keeps the downstream corpus consistent.

Step 02 — Translation

All downstream extraction is run on a harmonised Polish text field. Postings already detected as Polish are kept unchanged; English and other-language fields are translated into Polish using Gemma 3 Translate 4B. Both original and translated fields are retained so that analysts can inspect source text when reviewing specific matches.

This step is needed because the same skill can otherwise appear in several languages within one analytical sample. Translation makes skill extraction, job-title standardisation, and taxonomy matching operate on a common-language input rather than mixing Polish, English, and hybrid phrasing.

Step 03 — Skill-Sentence Filtering

Job descriptions contain many sentences that are not skill requirements: benefits, company history, application instructions, equal-opportunity statements, and legal clauses. Before mapping to skills, we isolate the sentences that actually describe required competences, tasks, tools, or knowledge.

We use a fine-tuned BERT-style sentence classifier based on the SkillLess approach. Each sentence is labelled as skill-relevant or non-skill. In this sample, roughly 40–60% of description text is filtered out before semantic matching. This improves precision because the ESCO matcher only sees sentences that plausibly contain skills.

Step 04 — ESCO Skill Mapping

Skill-relevant sentences are mapped to the European Skills, Competences, Qualifications and Occupations taxonomy (ESCO), which contains roughly 13,000 standardised skill and competence entries. ESCO provides the common language that makes job postings and BUR training descriptions comparable.

The matching model is a custom contrastive bi-encoder. It places job-ad sentences and ESCO skill labels in a shared embedding space: semantically matching pairs are pulled closer together, while non-matching pairs are pushed apart. For example, a sentence such as experience with SQL and data visualisation should be close to ESCO entries such as use query languages and manage databases, but far from unrelated labels such as negotiate contracts.

Hard negatives are central to training. The model must distinguish nearby but incorrect skills, such as use programming languages versus use query languages, not only obviously unrelated concepts. This makes the model better suited to real vacancy text, where employers describe skills in informal, overlapping, and sometimes ambiguous ways.

Candidate skills are ranked by cosine similarity. A calibrated similarity threshold is then applied to remove low-confidence matches and control the number of skills assigned to each posting or training description. The threshold is tuned on held-out benchmark data to balance precision and recall.

Step 05 — Job-Title Standardisation

Raw job titles are highly variable. The same role can appear as Inżynier oprogramowania, Backend Developer, Programista, Full-Stack Developer, or Senior Software Engineer. To support occupational analysis, titles are standardised to ESCO occupations.

Titles are first cleaned by removing common noise such as embedded locations, salaries, and seniority prefixes. Cleaned titles are embedded with a labour-market language model and matched to a pre-computed index of ESCO occupation labels using nearest-neighbour search. The best matching occupation and its similarity score are retained for downstream analysis and quality filtering.

Where a title is ambiguous, extracted skill context helps interpretation: two postings with the same generic title can map differently if their skill profiles imply different occupations.

Step 06 — Sector Classification (ISIC/NACE)

Sector analysis requires assigning postings to an economic activity. The pipeline maps standardised ESCO occupations to ISIC/NACE activity codes using the official ESCO-to-NACE crosswalk. At the two-digit division level used in this report, NACE Rev. 2.1 and ISIC Rev. 5 share the same division codes and boundaries, so results are directly comparable across the two systems.

The assignment uses three tiers. If an occupation maps to a single code, the assignment is deterministic. If all candidate codes share the same two-digit division, that division is assigned directly. If candidates span several divisions, the job title and description are compared with candidate sector labels using multilingual sentence embeddings, and the highest-scoring candidate is selected. A confidence margin is retained for auditing.

Validation and Benchmarking

The ESCO skill-matching component is benchmarked against the HOUSE and TECH datasets used in recent ESCO skill-extraction research (Decorte et al. (2025)). These datasets contain job postings annotated with gold-standard ESCO skill labels by human experts. Against these benchmarks, the pipeline improves reported RP@5 performance by roughly three percentage points relative to the current state of the art.

The benchmark is not a guarantee that every individual match is correct. Rather, it supports the use of the extracted skills for aggregate composition analysis: sectoral shares, regional shares, demand-supply mismatch, and robustness checks.
